title: Quantitative Endogenous Polyamine Analysis via Capillary Electrophoresis/Mass Spectrometry: Characterization and Practical Considerations

sections.abstract: Commonly used analytical techniques for polyamine analysis, including derivatization and mixed-mode liquid chromatography (LC), have inherent disadvantages. Capillary electrophoresis (CE) is uniquely suited to analyze small, highly charged molecules because analytes are separated on the basis of their electrophoretic mobility, not polarity or association with a stationary phase. Microfluidic CE–mass spectrometry (mCE–MS) is a relatively recent addition to commercially available CE offerings that streamlines traditional CE–MS interfacing and has the potential to improve upon classic CE challenges to robustness and reproducibility. MS instrument choice and scanning parameters are strongly influenced by a need for high acquisition rate to adequately sample CE peaks. Alternatively, isotachophoresis on loading can be intentionally avoided to produce sufficiently wide peaks. The mCE platform utilized here performed very well in many metrics; a limit of detection (LOD) as low as 0.25 ng/mL was achieved for spermidine, and endogenous spermidine was easily detected in blood with this method. Both of these are challenging tasks for any separation technique and demonstrate a strong use case for the platform. During experimentation, various idiosyncrasies in the commercial CE–MS interface resulted in extensive chip-to-chip variability in both peak shape and LOD, complicating the application to robust absolute quantitation. Practical guidance for similar analyses is provided.
sections.introduction:
Endogenous polyamines have garnered significant interest in fields related to aging, longevity, and metabolism due to their potential neuroprotective and autophagy-regulating effects [ 1 , 2 ]. Among these, spermidine is principally implicated in longevity and resistance to neurodegeneration and is commonly cited as a caloric restriction mimetic [ 3 , 4 ]. It is strongly correlated with increased lifespan and health span in a number of model systems [ 4 ], and significant recent work strives to further this relationship in human subjects [ 5 – 7 ]. Despite this, quantitative analysis of underivatized spermidine in biological matrices remains difficult to achieve with common liquid-phase separation and mass spectrometric techniques. The low mass and p K a of most polyamines significantly hamper traditional sample cleanup, separation, and analysis. Even mixed-mode liquid chromatography (LC) stationary phases or columns designed for specialty applications still necessitate significant method optimization for LC-based studies of polar metabolites like spermidine. Additionally, columns of this variety are often pH and salt sensitive, meaning that even slight day-to-day or run-to-run variations can lead to significant reproducibility issues.

Serum and plasma are traditionally the matrix chosen for polyamine analysis due to the relative ease of collection and analysis compared to whole blood. However, this choice risks an incomplete measurement of circulating spermidine content. Whole blood provides a much more holistic measurement, as the amount of spermidine in erythrocytes can dwarf that found in plasma [ 8 ]. Additionally, the ratio of spermidine found in these two reservoirs is not constant and can fluctuate widely due to disease state or simply among individuals [ 9 ]. Understandably, whole blood is inherently a more complex matrix, making the already difficult task of separation and detection considerably more involved.

For these reasons, an attractive alternative to LC can be found in capillary electrophoresis (CE). CE is compatible with mass spectrometry (MS) analysis but leverages a completely different mechanism to separate analytes. In CE, molecules are separated by their electrophoretic mobility, which depends on both the size and the charge of a molecule. Rather than using a parabolic flow through stationary and mobile phases, CE uses an electric field in a flat, electroosmotic plug flow to separate molecules. As polyamines are inherently highly charged, CE is well-suited for this analysis.

Microfluidic CE (mCE) devices have garnered academic interest since the mid-1990s but only recently have various mCE–MS platforms been commercialized with a focus on analyte separation and detection. Enthusiasm for the technique stems from the desire to improve upon many drawbacks commonly observed in traditional CE, namely, the low reproducibility, sensitivity, and the complicated interfacing with MS [ 10 ]. The ZipChip platform manufactured by 908 Devices was chosen for this work due to its integrated solution to the latter challenge [ 11 ]. The platform has been employed in the MS analysis of glycoproteins [ 12 , 13 ], intact antibodies [ 14 , 15 ], and, more recently, metabolites [ 16 ].

The ZipChip capillary consists of a microfluidic channel embedded within a glass slide. Samples and background electrolyte are introduced via PEEK plastic wells in the slide cover. Rather than being coupled to an electrospray ionization (ESI) emitter and accompanying high voltage for MS analysis, the ZipChip integrates the ESI source into the corner of the microfluidic chip. The entire channel is biased at a high voltage compared to the ion inlet, providing the potential difference needed for ESI and vastly simplifying the coupling from the user’s perspective. The chip is housed within a manifold that controls the separation and positions the ESI spray optimally to introduce ions into the mass spectrometer. More technical information can be found in the review by Naghdi et al. [ 17 ].

One major advantage brought by this new platform is efficiency; not only can separation be accomplished in minutes (a roughly 10-fold decrease in analysis time from traditional CE), but sample preparation time is also greatly reduced as desalting can be done on-chip [ 11 ]. Many samples can be analyzed with a “dilute and shoot” protocol, saving time and reducing the amount of analyte lost in a multi-step preparation. Here, we describe efforts to optimize and characterize an mCE–MS-based method for absolute quantitation of underivatized spermidine in whole blood.
sections.methods:
Methanol was purchased from Fisher Chemical (Hampton, NH). Spermidine and 1,6-diaminohexane were purchased from Millipore Sigma (Burlington, MA).

A ZipChip HR chip and ZipChip Peptides Kit, including the ZipChip Peptide BGE and sample diluent, were obtained from 908 Devices (Boston, MA). Out of necessity due to multiple chip failures, three different HR chips were compared during this analysis. Electric field strength was 300 V/cm, and injection volume was 5.5 nL. ZipChip pressure assist start time was set to 30 s.

For MS analysis, the Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was operated in positive parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) mode unless otherwise noted with an ESI spray voltage of 1500 V and ion transfer tube temperature of 280°C. Orbitrap mass resolution was set to 7500, and 1 microscan was used for averaging. PRM transitions were analyzed with an isolation window of 1 m/z and 40% HCD energy. Transitions for spermidine (parent ion at 146.1657 m/z used) were 112.112, 72.081, and 58.066 m/z . Transitions for 1,6-diaminohexane (parent mass at 117.1392 m/z used) were 100.113, 83.086, and 55.054 m/z .

The Orbitrap Q-Exactive HF (Thermo Fisher Scientific) analysis was initially carried out in positive mode MS 1 . ESI spray voltage was 2000 V, and mass range analyzed was 50–500 m/z . A capillary temperature of 275°C and S-lens RF level of 60 were chosen to increase analyte transmission through ion optics. The minimum possible resolution of 15 000 was used at an AGC target of 3E6. For MS 2 analysis, all ion fragmentations between 50 and 300 m/z were fragmented with normalized collisional energy of 55. For PRM analysis, the same fragments as above were selected for analysis.

Two sequential additions of 400 μL methanol spiked with 0.05 μg/mL 1,6-diaminohexane were added to 200 μL of whole blood. After vortexing, the samples were centrifuged at 16 000 × g for 10 min to pellet the precipitate, after which 500 μL of the supernatant was removed and dried using a vacuum concentrator. The sample was reconstituted in either diluent or background electrolyte for analysis.

Data visualization and spermidine quantitation were performed with Skyline version 22.2.0.351 and all default settings. Electropherograms were manually inspected to ensure appropriate peak-picking. A calibration curve was generated using a linear regression fit, normalized to the surrogate standard 1,6-diaminohexane.
sections.results:
Compared to LC separations, CE has relatively few parameters to change and optimize. Electric field was adjusted to maximize peak width and number of MS scans per analyte. Interestingly, although spermidine and the internal standard 1,6-diaminohexane individually had different migration times of 4.62 and 3.33 min, respectively ( Figure 1 ), when combined in one neat mix, they eluted at the same time ( Figure 2 ). The cause of this migration time shift when injected together is not known, but the phenomenon was consistent and apparent across multiple injections, days, microfluidic chips, manifolds, and samples. It is possible that this behavior is a result of stacking on injection or some other isotachophoresis-related behavior that arises from the high p K a and hydrophilicity of these compounds.

MS 1 information alone is insufficient to report metabolite assignments with high confidence in MS. For quantitative analysis in complex mixtures, PRM is a commonly used MS acquisition mode for targeted quantitation. It involves the analysis solely of known intact mass and fragment mass pairs for a targeted analyte list and can be used with a front-end separation technique to effectively quantitate target analytes in complex mixtures. Duty cycle and scan rate are parameters that must be well controlled to use PRM quantitatively, particularly in the context of CE–MS. Lower scan rates tend to produce a higher mass resolution or a lower limit of detection (LOD) but result in fewer mass spectra being acquired. During a chromatographic or CE separation, the peak shape and, most importantly, width must be considered when optimizing these parameters, as an ideal electrophoretic peak should be sampled at least 8–10 times in order to produce a reliable measurement of peak area. This is especially pertinent in CE–MS and mCE–MS, where peak shape cannot be assumed to be Gaussian.

Although the high-resolution separations offered by mCE–MS are often an advantage, the extremely narrow peaks that are generated by the flat electroosmotic flow are not always wide enough to collect the necessary 8–10 measurements per peak. This is demonstrated in Figure 3 , where the mCE–MS manifold was initially coupled to a Thermo Q-Exactive HF. This instrument has an Orbitrap mass analyzer, and with factory configuration, it can analyze with a minimum resolving power of 15 000. At the MS 1 and PRM mass ranges specified, this corresponds to a sampling rate of 12.0 and 10.4 spectra/s, respectively. The less-frequent scan rates in MS 2 measurements further exacerbate the poor peak sampling and prohibit reliable quantitation on the Q-Exactive HF. Despite attempts to slightly increase the peak width by lowering the electric field voltage, the sampling rate was simply too low to keep up with the fast mCE separation, resulting in too few scans collected for spermidine and 1,6-diaminohexane.

The Thermo Orbitrap Exploris 480 is an instrument with a newer Orbitrap mass analyzer and ion optics that can be operated at a lower resolution, down to 7500 with factory settings. Due to the Orbitrap principle of analysis involving the Fourier transform of signal harmonic in the time domain, halving the desired resolution increases the sampling rate by considerably more than twofold. The resolution of 7500 corresponds to a sampling rate of 50 scans/s in MS 1 , or 25 scans/s when performing two-compound PRM. When coupled to the Exploris 480, the mCE–MS analysis of spermidine and 1,6-diaminohexane yields well over 7–8 scans per peak, a number that allows for confident PRM-based quantitation.

Although in some cases, higher mass resolution is absolutely necessary, PRM or full MS 2 scans are often carried out on relatively low-resolution instruments, as the specificity endowed by measuring MS 2 transitions is often adequate for most cases. Thus, it is not expected that lowering mass resolution will significantly impact the specificity of the analysis. This is, however, a conclusion each user must verify for themselves.

Worth mentioning is the fact that newer Orbitrap systems like the Exploris handle ion transmission, isolation, and analysis in a true PRM fashion, which involves a separate dwell time for each analyte specified. This is why the scan rate halves when comparing MS 1 and two-compound PRM on the Exploris 480 but only drops a fraction on the Q-Exactive. This also means that the scan rate decreases further for every analyte isolated. A four-compound PRM scan on the Exploris again halves the scan rate to 12.5 scans/s. To avoid issues when analyzing a higher number of compounds, the instrument should instead be operated in full MS 2 mode, and traditional MS 2 quantitation could be performed. Under the conditions specified above, this is analyte agnostic and produces a scan rate of 25 MS 2 scans/s on the Exploris 480, a reasonable alternative to PRM when there are greater than two compounds of interest.

MS duty cycle/sampling rate is the first candidate for adjustment if higher peak sampling is required. If this variable is not a tunable parameter due to lack of available MS instrumentation, the degree of isotachophoresis on sample loading is another variable that may be probed to improve peak sampling. A major analytical strength of certain mCE loading methods is the transient isotachophoresis, or sample stacking, that is, performed at the beginning of a CE separation prior to the sample entering the microfluidic channel. This results in an extremely thin sample plug being introduced to the channel that can increase sensitivity and lower LOD [ 18 ]. However, this is accomplished through the narrowing of the analyte bands, thereby increasing the local concentration upon detection but leading to extremely narrow peaks.

Transient isotachophoresis requires the presence of a higher mobility salt in the loading buffer compared to the running background electrolyte. The proprietary diluent included with a ZipChip kit contains an electrolyte solution with higher electrophoretic mobility than the background electrolyte to produce the isotachophoresis upon loading. To avoid this intended sample stacking and encourage wider peaks, the sample can be reconstituted in the background electrolyte instead. This allows the bands to diffuse during loading and analysis, widening the peaks that reach the detector. The difference in the peak width is readily apparent, with a significant increase in the number of MS scans collected in PRM analysis ( Figure 4A ). An unexpected but welcome product of using background electrolyte as the reconstitution solvent is that separation can also be achieved between spermidine and 1,6-diaminohexane, something that is not possible otherwise.

A convenient advantage of mCE is the lack of sample preparation required. Many samples can be analyzed directly without the need for solid-phase extraction or other methods of sample cleanup. ESI is a competitive ionization mechanism, making this ionization technique incompatible with high concentrations of salts or surfactants as these species outcompete and suppress analytes for the limited charge available. Because the ZipChip manifold uses a pressure-driven injection, samples can be desalted on the chip, negating the need for manual desalting prior to analysis.

Whole blood spermidine levels are typically reported around 2 μg/mL, well above the LOD achievable with mCE–MS [ 19 ]. After being diluted in background electrolyte, spermidine was easily detected in whole blood even without sample stacking ( Figure 4B ).

mCE is attractive in large part because it potentially provides strategies to address limitations inherent in classical CE, namely, lack of reproducibility and utility in absolute quantitation. These shortcomings have resulted in the siloing of capillary zone electrophoresis as a niche technique not well suited for large-scale adoption where reproducibility and rigorous accounting are required such as qualified pharmaceutical work. It was hoped that this larger focus on reproducibility in mCE would allow for reliable absolute quantitation of biomolecules that are difficult to study via other separation techniques.

A partial calibration curve was collected on one chip ( Figure 5 ) with an R 2 of 0.9807 and a relative standard deviation between replicates of less than 5%, but only four points were collected prior to complete chip failure. The ZipChip manifold is capable of impressively low LODs and facile sample preparation in ideal conditions but was found to suffer from significant chip-to-chip variability. A 100 ng/mL spermidine standard analyzed on three different chips returned very different peak shapes, limits of detection, and migration times ( Figure 6A ), although resolution of spermidine and 1,6-diaminohexane was found to be reproducible.

Peak shape is the most noticeable characteristic expressed differently between chips. The three different peak shapes obtained from three different microfluidic chips presumably indicate inconsistencies in the channel characteristics. These could conceivably result from differences in channel shape or dimensions but most likely indicate that the channel coating and treatment are not consistent in dissuading analyte adsorption or are regulating electroosmotic flow with varying degrees of success. Chip 3 has the most significantly different peak shape, but this could be due to sample loading requirements. This chip provided a much lower signal than the previous pair, and as such significantly higher sample concentrations were required. As a result, direct comparison to the first two chips is improper as sample concentration could conceivably be a large contributor to the peak shape observed.

This disparity in LOD from chip to chip was also observed to persist through multiple pairs. The lowest LOD achieved on a ZipChip was an impressive 0.25 ng/mL, but another chip tested had an LOD nearly three orders of magnitude higher ( Figure 6B ). A change of this magnitude implies not simply a discrepancy in the microfluidic channel, but presumably an inconsistency in the ESI source of the chip as well. Concerning differences in the baseline noise and signal are also readily apparent. Chip 1 has an expected baseline signal. The noise is considerably low in intensity and variability, and these two parameters lend reassurance that chip spray is stable, robust, and ion transmission into and through the instrument is reliable. Chip 2, on the other hand, has a baseline intensity of zero. Although this may be attractive in theory (and in this case does result in a lower LOD), in practice, it indicates that chip spray may not be robust, and ions are not reliably being introduced through the electrospray. Indeed, this chip’s electrospray was found to falter and become compromised only a handful of injections later.

This unpredictable lifetime of the microfluidic chips compounds the chip-to-chip variability detailed above. The chips have a rated lifetime of 125 injections but rarely reach that limit before the ESI spray becomes compromised ( Figure 7 ). This was found to occur even when standards and manufacturer-provided reagents, buffers, and best practices are utilized. Although Chip 1 lasted for 45 injections before failure, Chip 3 only completed 10 injections before the loss of the ESI spray, and no chip approached the intended 125-injection lifetime. The cause of the chip failure is not immediately clear, although it may be due to the degradation of the hydrophobic coating used on the chip. Once this occurs, it is difficult and often impossible to recover the electrospray even if the coating is reapplied by the user. With the wide variability found in both peak shape and LOD, this would necessitate restarting an analysis rather than simply continuing with a new microfluidic chip.
